pos: n. (the surrounding of a city by an army to reduce it; rendering Hebrew matsor, from tsur, to bind or besiege)
etymology: From Old French sege, a seat, from the Latin sedeo, to sit — an army sits down before a city. The buried image is patience rather than assault: a siege wins by staying.
biblical_def: A siege in Scripture is judgment made slow. Ezekiel is commanded to act one out in miniature against a tile: “lay siege against it, and build a fort against it, and cast a mount against it; set the camp also against it, and set battering rams against it round about” (Ezekiel 4:2). The prophet becomes the besieger of his own city, and the accumulation of clauses is the point — a siege is methodical, and Jerusalem's fall would be too. Isaiah puts the LORD himself in the besieger's place: “I will camp against thee round about, and will lay siege against thee with a mount” (Isaiah 29:3). This is the hardest fact about the sieges of the Old Testament: the army outside the wall is often God's instrument against his own people, and the walls that were meant to keep enemies out become the enclosure of a judgment. The historian records the end without adornment: “And the city was besieged unto the eleventh year of king Zedekiah” (2 Kings 25:2) — one sentence covering months of famine. Micah writes from inside one: “he hath laid siege against us: they shall smite the judge of Israel with a rod upon the cheek” (Micah 5:1). The very next verse names Bethlehem and the ruler whose goings forth have been from everlasting. The promise of Christ is given to a people under siege.
webster_summary: The sitting-down of an army before a city. In Scripture it is judgment made slow and methodical, often with the LORD himself named as the besieger of his own city — and Micah announces Bethlehem from inside one.
webster_full: SIEGE, n. [Fr. siege, a seat; L. sedeo, to sit.] The setting of an army around or before a fortified place for the purpose of compelling the garrison to surrender.
2. Any continued endeavor to gain possession.
3. Formerly, a seat; a throne; hence, rank; place; class.
4. To lay siege, to besiege; to beset with an armed force.
5. To raise a siege, to relinquish an attempt to take a place by besieging it.
corruption_summary: The sieges of Scripture are read as ancient military history rather than as the covenant sanctions God warned of by name — and the God who besieges his own city is quietly replaced by one who only ever rescues.
corruption_paragraphs: Deuteronomy 28 lists siege among the covenant curses in appalling detail, centuries before Nebuchadnezzar's engineers arrived, and Leviticus 26 does the same. When the Babylonian mount went up against Jerusalem it was not an accident of geopolitics but the arrival of a stated sanction. Modern readings that treat these narratives as the ordinary fate of small kingdoms between empires lose exactly what the prophets insisted on — that Israel's political history was covenantal, and that the besieging army was a rod in the hand of her God. Isaiah 29:3 will not let the reader escape it: the speaker who camps against Ariel round about is the LORD.

The principle to recover is where the promise falls. Micah 5:1 describes a judge of Israel struck on the cheek with a rod while the enemy sits outside the wall; Micah 5:2 announces the everlasting ruler to come out of Bethlehem Ephratah. God gives his brightest promise to a people at their lowest, and does not wait for the siege to lift before speaking of the Messiah. A church that has learned to read sieges rightly will neither pretend the judgment is not real nor conclude that God has finished with the city he is chastening.
roots_summary: Hebrew matsor is a siege or the works of one, from tsur, to bind, confine, besiege. Dayeq is the siege-wall thrown up; solelah, the mount cast against a wall.

pos: n. pl. (that which binds — fetters, bonds, ligaments; also a company of men bound together; rendering Hebrew moserah, Greek desmos and sundesmos)
etymology: From the Saxon band, from bindan, to bind. The same word gives both a fetter and a company — men bound together in one troop — and the KJV uses both senses freely.
biblical_def: Bands are whatever binds, and Scripture turns the word four ways. It is the rebel's name for God's rule: the kings of the earth take counsel together and say, “Let us break their bands asunder, and cast away their cords from us” (Psalm 2:3). The doctrine in that verse is that submission to the LORD and his Anointed feels like bondage to a heart in revolt, and that the revolt is against a yoke which is in fact life. It is God's own manner of drawing: “I drew them with cords of a man, with bands of love: and I was to them as they that take off the yoke on their jaws” (Hosea 11:4). God binds, but the cords are love and the effect is the easing of a yoke, not its tightening. It is what the gospel breaks: in the Philippian jail “immediately all the doors were opened, and every one's bands were loosed” (Acts 16:26) — and remarkably, nobody ran. Paul uses the anatomical sense for the church: the body, “from which all the body by joints and bands having nourishment ministered, and knit together, increaseth with the increase of God” (Colossians 2:19). Here bands are ligaments, and the argument is against a false teaching that had let go the Head. A church coheres by connection to Christ, and its growth is the increase of God.
webster_summary: That which binds — fetters, ligaments, or a bound company. Psalm 2 calls God's rule bands to be broken; Hosea calls his drawing bands of love; Colossians makes them the ligaments by which a body holds to its Head.
webster_full: BAND, n. [Sax. band, from bindan, to bind.] A fillet; a cord; a tie; a chain; any narrow ligament with which a thing is bound.
2. Figuratively, any chain; any means of restraint; that which draws or confines.
3. Means of union or connection between persons; as the bands of society.
4. A company of men united in any common design; a body of soldiers.
5. In anatomy, a ligament by which parts are bound together.
corruption_summary: God's commands are experienced as bands to be broken — the exact sentiment of Psalm 2:3 — and autonomy is called freedom, while the bands that actually bind a church to Christ are quietly loosed.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 2:3 is the most modern verse in the Psalter, because it states the assumption of the age in the age's own accent: God's law is a restraint on the self, and maturity consists in shaking it off. Scripture does not answer this by denying that the law binds. It answers by asking what happens next. The psalm's reply is that he who sitteth in the heavens shall laugh, and then that the Son is to be kissed lest he be angry — and it closes, unexpectedly, with a beatitude: blessed are all they that put their trust in him. The bands turn out to be the boundary of blessedness, and outside them is not liberty but the perishing from the way.

The principle to recover is Colossians 2:19, where bands are not fetters at all but ligaments. Paul is describing a teacher who had let go the Head — and the consequence is not that the body becomes free but that it stops being nourished and stops growing. The image is exact and physical: a limb detached from the body does not gain independence. Every doctrine that promises a church growth by loosening its connection to Christ and his word is promising the vitality of a severed arm.
roots_summary: Hebrew moserah is a bond or fetter, from asar, to bind. Greek desmos is a bond or fetter; sundesmos is a joint ligament, the word of Colossians 2:19.

Hebrew aboth (H5688) — a cord or rope, twisted; the cords of a man in Hosea 11:4.

usage: Of rebellion against God's rule: let us break their bands asunder (Psalm 2:3).

Of the ligaments of the body of Christ: by joints and bands having nourishment ministered (Colossians 2:19).

pos: n. (a payment exacted by a sovereign or a conqueror; rendering Hebrew mas and middah, Greek kensos and phoros)
etymology: From the Latin tributum, that which is paid, from tribuo, to assign or allot — itself from tribus, a tribe, the unit by which the levy was assessed. Tribute is a tax paid upward by the subjected.
biblical_def: Tribute is money paid by the weaker to the stronger, and Scripture records it first as a sign of a job left undone: “when Israel was strong, that they put the Canaanites to tribute, and did not utterly drive them out” (Judges 1:28). Israel chose revenue over obedience, and the nations they taxed became the snare that ruined them. The word then follows the nation into subjection, where the enemies of the rebuilding write to Artaxerxes warning that a restored Jerusalem will not “pay toll, tribute, and custom” (Ezra 4:13) — the accusation that a people who worship God will not pay their taxes is very old and was false then too. The decisive passage is our Lord's. Asked “Doth not your master pay tribute?” (Matthew 17:24), he first establishes the principle that the children of a king are free, and then sends Peter for a coin in a fish's mouth so as not to give offence. He is under no obligation and pays anyway. Paul turns this into a standing command: “Render therefore to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due; custom to whom custom; fear to whom fear; honour to whom honour” (Romans 13:7) — and the magistrate he was commanding Christians to pay was Nero's.
webster_summary: A payment exacted by a sovereign or conqueror. Judges shows Israel taking tribute instead of obeying; Christ, though free, pays lest he offend; Paul commands it be rendered even to a pagan magistrate.
webster_full: TRIBUTE, n. [L. tributum, from tribuo, to give, bestow or divide.] An annual or stated sum of money or other valuable thing, paid by one prince or nation to another, either as an acknowledgment of submission, or for the purchase of peace.
2. A personal contribution; as a tribute of respect.
3. Something given or contributed; as a tribute of praise.
4. TRIBUTARY, a. Paying tribute to another, either from compulsion or to secure protection.
5. In Scripture, tribute money, the didrachma paid for the service of the temple, Matt. 17.
corruption_summary: Romans 13 is pressed into two errors at once — made a warrant for unlimited obedience to the state, or dismissed as a first-century accommodation with nothing to say to citizens today.
corruption_paragraphs: Romans 13:7 stands inside a passage that grants the magistrate real authority as God's minister, and it has been used to demand from Christians a submission Scripture does not require. The limit is set elsewhere and plainly: the same apostles who wrote it told the council we ought to obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29), and the midwives, Daniel, and the three in Babylon are all commended for refusing a command. The state is one of three God-ordained authorities alongside family and church, each with its own sphere, and it exceeds itself when it legislates in another's. The opposite error waves the passage away as advice for a persecuted minority with no power. But Paul wrote of the empire that would kill him, and did not make the magistrate's character the condition of the payment.

The principle to recover is our Lord's own reasoning at Capernaum. He argues that the sons are free — and then pays, lest we should offend them (Matthew 17:27). Liberty is real and is voluntarily not pressed. That is a temper almost entirely lost in public argument, where a right, once established, is thought to require exercising. The Son of God had a better claim to exemption than any citizen ever will, and he sent for the coin.
roots_summary: Hebrew mas is a levy of forced labour or tax; middah, tribute or toll. Greek kensos is the census-tax; phoros, tribute paid by a subject people.

Hebrew middah (H4061) — tribute, toll; the Aramaic term in the letters of Ezra 4.
Greek kensos (G2778) — the poll-tax or census tax; render unto Caesar the things that are Caesar's.
Greek phoros (G5411) — tribute paid by a subject nation; the word in Romans 13:7.

pos: n. (one who rules under a higher authority; a provincial ruler; also a pilot or steersman; rendering Hebrew pechah, Greek hegemon and kubernetes)
etymology: From the Latin gubernator, a steersman, from the Greek kubernao, to steer a ship. The oldest sense is nautical, and English kept it: a governor is a man at a helm, which is exactly the image James 3:4 uses.
biblical_def: A governor in Scripture rules under someone else, and the office runs from Joseph to Pilate. Joseph, sold as a slave, becomes the man “governor over the land, and he it was that sold to all the people of the land” (Genesis 42:6) — and his brethren bow before him without knowing him, which is the exact fulfilment of the dream they had hated. Zerubbabel is “governor of Judah” (Haggai 1:1), a son of David's line ruling a province for a Persian king; the word of the LORD comes to him and to Joshua the high priest together, prince and priest side by side over a small returned people. And the New Testament uses the title for the man who condemned the Lord: “they led him away, and delivered him to Pontius Pilate the governor” (Matthew 27:2). A governor holds delegated power, which is why Christ could tell Pilate that he would have none at all against him except it were given him from above. James keeps the nautical root and makes it an image of the tongue: great ships driven of fierce winds “are turned about with a very small helm, whithersoever the governor listeth” (James 3:4). Small things steer large ones. That is true of a rudder, of a tongue, and of the men God sets in office.
webster_summary: One who rules under a higher authority — Joseph in Egypt, Zerubbabel in Judah, Pilate in Judaea — and, keeping the word's nautical root, the steersman whose small helm turns a great ship.
webster_full: GOVERNOR, n. [L. gubernator, from guberno, to steer.] One who governs; one invested with supreme authority.
2. One who is invested with the supreme executive authority of a state or community.
3. A tutor; one who has the care of a young man; one who instructs and forms the manners.
4. A pilot; one who steers a ship.
5. In Scripture, a ruler of a province under a king; as Pontius Pilate the governor, Matt. 27.
corruption_summary: Authority is treated as ultimate rather than delegated, so that officeholders act as though power originated with them — the exact assumption Christ corrected in Pilate.
corruption_paragraphs: Pilate's claim was the ordinary claim of office: knowest thou not that I have power to crucify thee, and have power to release thee? Our Lord's answer draws the line the whole biblical doctrine of government rests on — Thou couldest have no power at all against me, except it were given thee from above (John 19:10-11). Every governor is a governor under God, and the etymology preaches it: a steersman does not own the ship or choose the sea. A magistrate who forgets this becomes a tyrant in principle before he becomes one in practice, and citizens who forget it either idolise the state or despise it, both of which follow from thinking the power is the officeholder's own.

The principle to recover is the way God's purpose runs straight through pagan administration. Joseph governs Egypt for a Pharaoh; Zerubbabel governs Judah for a Persian; Pilate condemns Christ for Rome — and in each case the providence of God is accomplished by men who had no notion they were serving it. This is the classical two-kingdoms position rightly held: Christ is Lord of all spheres, the civil magistrate has a real and God-given office in his own, and the church does not need to capture the state to be sure God is governing through it.
roots_summary: Hebrew pechah is a provincial governor under a foreign crown. Greek hegemon is a leader or prefect; kubernetes is a steersman, the nautical root of the English word.

Greek kubernetes (G2942) — a steersman, pilot; the governor of the ship in James 3:4.

pos: n. pl. (men appointed to a charge under authority; in Israel, scribes and marshals set with the judges; rendering Hebrew shoter, Greek huperetes)
etymology: From the Latin officium, a duty or service, from opus and facio, to do a work. Hebrew shoter is from a root meaning to write or set in order — the officers were originally the keepers of the registers, and so the men who summoned and marshalled.
biblical_def: Officers in Israel were subordinate appointees who made rule workable. Moses is told to gather seventy elders “whom thou knowest to be the elders of the people, and officers over them” (Numbers 11:16), so the office existed before Sinai's administration was complete. The law then makes it permanent alongside the judges: “Judges and officers shalt thou make thee in all thy gates, which the LORD thy God giveth thee, throughout thy tribes: and they shall judge the people with just judgment” (Deuteronomy 16:18). Two things are notable. Justice is to be local — in all thy gates, not in a capital only — and the standard is fixed by God rather than by the officers. David's reorganisation gives numbers: “six thousand were officers and judges” (1 Chronicles 23:4), a substantial civil service drawn from the Levites. The New Testament uses the word for the temple guard, and gives them one of the finest lines in the Gospels. Sent to arrest Jesus, they come back empty-handed, and to the Pharisees' demand for an explanation they answer: “Never man spake like this man” (John 7:46). Working men, sent to do a job, disarmed by preaching — and their report is a better Christology than their masters'.
webster_summary: Men appointed under authority. Deuteronomy sets judges and officers in every gate with a fixed standard of justice; the temple officers sent to arrest Christ return with the confession, Never man spake like this man.
webster_full: OFFICER, n. [Fr. officier, from L. officium, duty.] A person commissioned or authorized to perform any public duty.
2. A commissioned or non-commissioned man in military service.
3. One who holds an office; a person invested with authority in a particular department.
4. In Scripture, an inferior magistrate or attendant on a judge; judges and officers shalt thou make thee, Deut. 16.
5. Also, an attendant of the priests and elders; the officers sent to take him, John 7.
corruption_summary: Justice is centralised and professionalised, so that the local gate where Deuteronomy set it disappears — and the officers' honest testimony in John 7 is treated as naivety rather than as evidence.
corruption_paragraphs: Deuteronomy 16:18 puts judges and officers in all thy gates, which is to say justice was to be administered where people lived, by men their neighbours knew, under a standard none of them wrote. This is a real political principle and it has been steadily eroded wherever judgment migrates upward to distant and unaccountable bodies. Scripture's own guardrails follow immediately: no wresting of judgment, no respect of persons, no taking of a gift, because a gift blinds the eyes of the wise (Deuteronomy 16:19). The safeguard is not that officers are good men but that the rule they administer is not theirs and the people they answer to are near.

The principle to recover is in the officers' report. The Pharisees answer them with contempt — Are ye also deceived? have any of the rulers or of the Pharisees believed on him? — and the argument is entirely from credentials. The officers had offered evidence: they had heard him. Nicodemus then asks whether the law judges a man before it hears him, and is dismissed with a sneer about Galilee. The whole exchange is a study in how learned men insulate themselves from testimony they do not want, and how God is pleased to put a true confession in the mouth of the men sent to do the arresting.

pos: n. pl. (chiefs or clan-heads, in the KJV chiefly of Edom; rendering Hebrew alluph, a chief of a thousand)
etymology: From the Latin dux, a leader, through Old French duc. The translators chose the English feudal title to render Hebrew alluph, a tribal chieftain — a leader of a clan or of a thousand, from eleph, a thousand.
biblical_def: The dukes of the Authorized Version are chiefly Esau's. Genesis 36 is a long roll of them: “These were dukes of the sons of Esau… duke Teman, duke Omar, duke Zepho, duke Kenaz” (Genesis 36:15), and the Chronicler repeats the list (1 Chronicles 1:51). The placement is instructive, because Genesis gives Esau a chapter of established chiefs while Jacob's line is still a household of shepherds in a land they do not own. The rejected brother prospers visibly and early. Scripture is unembarrassed by this and does not hurry to correct the impression — it simply keeps telling the story. The Song of the Sea then names them among those who melt: “Then the dukes of Edom shall be amazed; the mighty men of Moab, trembling shall take hold upon them; all the inhabitants of Canaan shall melt away” (Exodus 15:15). The chiefs who had a chapter to themselves are, one book later, a line in the terror of the nations at what God did at the sea. The word is also used of Midian's chiefs, slain with Balaam: they “were dukes of Sihon, dwelling in the country” (Joshua 13:21). Established rank is not, in Scripture, a comment on divine favour.
webster_summary: Clan-chiefs, in the KJV chiefly Esau's. Genesis gives the rejected brother a chapter of dukes while Jacob is still landless — and the Song of the Sea shows the same dukes amazed at what God did for the shepherds.
webster_full: DUKE, n. [Fr. duc; L. dux, a leader, from duco, to lead.] In Great Britain, one of the highest order of nobility; a title of honor next below the princes.
2. In some countries on the continent, a sovereign prince, without the title of king.
3. A chief; a prince; as the dukes of Edom, Gen. 36.
4. DUKEDOM, n. The seignory or possessions of a duke; the territory of a duke.
5. Formerly, a leader or commander of an army.
corruption_summary: Visible rank and early prosperity are read as evidence of divine favour, though Genesis deliberately gives the chiefs and the genealogies to the rejected line while the chosen one waits.
corruption_paragraphs: The prosperity teaching that measures God's blessing by present standing has to skip Genesis 36 entirely. Esau, the brother of whom it is written Esau have I hated (Malachi 1:2-3; Romans 9:13), receives a full chapter of dukes, kings, and settled territory, and receives it before Israel has a foot of ground. Asaph felt the difficulty acutely and wrote a psalm about it — he was envious at the foolish when he saw the prosperity of the wicked, until he went into the sanctuary of God, and then understood I their end (Psalm 73:3, 17). Scripture's answer to visible prosperity in the ungodly is not denial but patience about endings.

The principle to recover is the reversal in Exodus 15:15. The dukes of Edom are named there not as powers but as men amazed, and what amazed them was a deliverance granted to slaves. God's election runs on other lines than rank: the younger over the elder, the shepherd over the chief, a nation of brickmakers over a settled aristocracy. Paul draws exactly this conclusion — God has chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty, that no flesh should glory in his presence (1 Corinthians 1:27-29).
roots_summary: Hebrew alluph is a chief or clan-head, from eleph, a thousand — the leader of a thousand. It is also used of a familiar friend or guide.
roots_lines: Hebrew alluph (H441) — a chief, a captain of a thousand; the KJV duke in Genesis 36.
Hebrew eleph (H505) — a thousand; the root of the chief's title.
Hebrew nasi (H5387) — a prince, one lifted up; the title of the tribal princes of Israel.
Hebrew rosh (H7218) — a head, chief; the common term for the head of a father's house.
Greek hegemon (G2232) — a leader; the Septuagint term used where the Hebrew has alluph.
usage: Of the roll of Esau's chiefs: these were dukes of the sons of Esau (Genesis 36:15).
Of those chiefs amazed at the sea: then the dukes of Edom shall be amazed (Exodus 15:15).

pos: n. pl. (a register of events in order of time; the state annals of a kingdom; rendering Hebrew dibre hayyamim, the words of the days)
etymology: From the Greek chronika, annals, from chronos, time. The Hebrew title is plainer and better: dibre hayyamim, the words of the days — a record of what the days themselves said.
biblical_def: The chronicles of Scripture are official annals, and the historical books refer to them constantly as sources standing outside the canon: “the rest of the acts of Jeroboam, how he warred, and how he reigned, behold, they are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel” (1 Kings 14:19), and the same formula closes reign after reign (1 Kings 15:31). This is worth pausing over. Inspired Scripture openly cites uninspired records, and does so without anxiety — the Holy Ghost employed real archives, and the writers used ordinary historical sources under his superintendence. Verbal plenary inspiration has never meant that the human authors received everything by dictation with their eyes shut; Luke likewise says he had perfect understanding of all things from the first (Luke 1:3). Nehemiah cites the same kind of register for the Levites (Nehemiah 12:23). The Chronicler even records a gap in the archive with an explanation attached: Joab began to number Israel but did not finish, “because there fell wrath for it against Israel; neither was the number put in the account of the chronicles of king David” (1 Chronicles 27:24). And in Esther the annals become providence's instrument — a sleepless king, a book read aloud at night, and a forgotten service to the crown remembered at exactly the hour Haman's gallows stood ready.
webster_summary: Official annals — the Hebrew calls them the words of the days. Scripture cites these uninspired records openly, and in Esther a night reading of the chronicles becomes the hinge of a deliverance.
webster_full: CHRONICLE, n. [Gr. chronika, from chronos, time.] A historical account of facts or events disposed in the order of time.
2. That which contains a chronological register of events; a history.
3. In the plural, the name of two books of the Old Testament.
4. CHRONICLE, v.t. To record in history or annals; to register.
5. CHRONICLER, n. A writer of a chronicle; a recorder of events in the order of time.
corruption_summary: Scripture's open use of ordinary archives is turned into an argument against its inspiration, as though a book that consulted sources could not be the word of God.
corruption_paragraphs: Historical-critical scholarship has often treated the source citations of Kings and Chronicles as evidence of a merely human compilation — a redactor stitching annals together, whose theological verdicts on the kings are later editorial overlay to be peeled away. The doctrine of inspiration does not require the conclusion and does not fear the evidence. Verbal plenary inspiration means that what the human authors wrote, God caused to be written, and it is no reduction of that to say the writers consulted registers, arranged material, and named their sources. The claim that the Chronicler's theological judgments are a later imposition is the assumption doing the work, not a finding: those judgments are the point of the book, and Scripture presents them as God's assessment of each reign, not as one interpretation among several.

The principle to recover is what Esther does with a book of annals. There is no miracle in that chapter, and God is not named anywhere in the book — there is only a king who cannot sleep, an attendant who reads the chronicles aloud, and a record of Mordecai's unrewarded loyalty reaching the royal ear on the one night it could save a nation. Providence works through archives, insomnia, and paperwork. A believer who can see God only in the spectacular will miss most of what he actually does.
roots_summary: Hebrew dibre hayyamim is literally the words of the days, the title of the books we call Chronicles. Zikkaron is a memorial or record; sepher, a book or scroll.
roots_lines: Hebrew dibre hayyamim (H1697 with H3117) — the words of the days; the Hebrew title of Chronicles.
Hebrew sepher (H5612) — a book, scroll, or written register; the book of the chronicles.
Hebrew zikkaron (H2146) — a memorial, a record kept for remembrance; the book of records in Esther 6.
Greek chronos (G5550) — time, duration; the root of the English title.
Greek Paraleipomena — the things left out, the Septuagint's name for Chronicles.
usage: Of the closing formula for a reign: they are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel (1 Kings 14:19).
Of a Levitical register: were written in the book of the chronicles (Nehemiah 12:23).
Of a deliberate gap in the record: neither was the number put in the account of the chronicles of king David (1 Chronicles 27:24).

pos: n. and v. (a pile; a ruin; to pile up; rendering Hebrew gal and ned, Greek soreuo)
etymology: From the Saxon heap, a crowd or pile. Hebrew gal is a heap of stones, from galal, to roll; ned is a heap of water standing up, used only of the sea and the Jordan divided.
biblical_def: A heap in Scripture is either a monument, a ruin, or a miracle. As monument it marks a judgment: over Achan “they raised over him a great heap of stones unto this day” (Joshua 7:26), and the place was named the valley of Achor, that is, Trouble. As ruin it is the fate of a city under the ban: “Joshua burnt Ai, and made it an heap for ever, even a desolation unto this day” (Joshua 8:28), and Isaiah pronounces the same of a great capital — Damascus “shall be a ruinous heap” (Isaiah 17:1). As miracle it is the sea itself: “He divided the sea, and caused them to pass through; and he made the waters to stand as an heap” (Psalm 78:13). Hebrew ned is reserved for that — water piled up and holding, which is no more natural than a mountain of loose stones standing without mortar, and is a picture of creation obeying its Maker against its own nature. The New Testament gives the word a final and startling turn. Paul, quoting Proverbs, commands kindness to an enemy: “if thine enemy hunger, feed him; if he thirst, give him drink: for in so doing thou shalt heap coals of fire on his head” (Romans 12:20). The heap a Christian is told to build is not a cairn over a punished man but a fire of undeserved kindness, and the aim named in the next verse is to overcome evil with good.
webster_summary: A pile, a ruin, or waters standing up. Scripture heaps stones over judgment, leaves cities as heaps, piles the sea into a wall — and commands the believer to heap coals of kindness on an enemy's head.
webster_full: HEAP, n. [Sax. heap, a crowd.] A pile or mass; a collection of things laid in a body, or thrown together so as to form an elevation.
2. A crowd; a throng; a cluster.
3. A mass of ruins; as, the city was made a heap.
4. HEAP, v.t. To throw or lay in a heap; to pile.
5. To amass; to accumulate; to lay up; as, to heap up treasures.
corruption_summary: Romans 12:20 is read as a permitted revenge — kindness deployed to shame an enemy — when Paul's own next sentence names the aim as overcoming evil with good.
corruption_paragraphs: A popular reading takes the coals of fire as a way of getting one's own back righteously: be kind, and your enemy will burn with shame. That misses Paul's framing at both ends. Before it he has written avenge not yourselves… for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord (Romans 12:19) — vengeance is not abolished, it is reassigned, and taken out of the believer's hands precisely because God will see to it. After it he writes Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good (Romans 12:21). Kindness used as a weapon of humiliation is simply vengeance with better manners, and it is not what stands between those two verses.

The principle to recover is the difference between the heaps. Israel piled stones over Achan and named the place Trouble, and the monument was a permanent public judgment. The Christian is given no such cairn to build. What he is handed instead is bread for a hungry enemy and water for a thirsty one, and the fire he kindles is meant to melt rather than to bury. Psalm 78:13 stands behind both: the God who made the waters stand up in a heap is entirely able to handle the vengeance, which is exactly why his people can afford to feed the men who hate them.
roots_summary: Hebrew gal is a heap of stones, from galal, to roll; ned is a heap of standing water, used of the sea and Jordan; tel is a mound of ruins.

Hebrew ned (H5067) — a heap of water standing up; used only of the divided sea and Jordan.
Hebrew tel (H8510) — a mound, a heap of ruins; a city made an heap for ever.
Hebrew galal (H1556) — to roll; the root behind the rolled-together heap of stones.
Greek soreuo (G4987) — to heap up, to pile on; the verb of Romans 12:20.
usage: Of a monument over judgment: they raised over him a great heap of stones (Joshua 7:26).
Of the waters piled up at the sea: he made the waters to stand as an heap (Psalm 78:13).
Of kindness to an enemy: thou shalt heap coals of fire on his head (Romans 12:20).

pos: n. (the cutting side of a blade; a border or brink; rendering Hebrew peh, the mouth, and qatseh, an end)
etymology: From the Saxon ecg, a point or blade, cognate with the Latin acies. The Hebrew idiom is vivid and untranslatable directly: a sword's edge is its mouth, and to be slain by the sword is to be eaten by it.
biblical_def: The commonest edge in the Authorized Version is a sword's, and the Hebrew calls it the sword's mouth. “And Joshua discomfited Amalek and his people with the edge of the sword” (Exodus 17:13) — the battle fought below while Moses' hands were held up above, so that the edge did the work and the intercession won it. Hebrews sets the phrase in its roll of faith among things faith did: some “escaped the edge of the sword, out of weakness were made strong, waxed valiant in fight” (Hebrews 11:34) — and the same chapter, a few lines later, records that others were sawn asunder and slain with the sword. Faith delivers from the edge and faith goes under it, and Hebrews will not let the reader choose only one list. Jeremiah uses the word in the proverb he abolishes: “The fathers have eaten a sour grape, and the children's teeth are set on edge” (Jeremiah 31:29) — a saying by which Judah excused itself as suffering for its ancestors' sins, and which the new covenant answers with personal responsibility. And Ecclesiastes gives the practical proverb: “If the iron be blunt, and he do not whet the edge, then must he put to more strength: but wisdom is profitable to direct” (Ecclesiastes 10:10). Effort cannot make up for a dull tool; wisdom is sharpening.
webster_summary: The cutting side of a blade — in Hebrew, the sword's mouth. Faith both escapes the edge and falls to it; Jeremiah abolishes the proverb of teeth set on edge; Ecclesiastes makes wisdom the whetting of the tool.
webster_full: EDGE, n. [Sax. ecg; L. acies.] In a general sense, the extreme border or point of any thing.
2. The cutting side of an instrument; as the edge of an ax or razor.
3. The abstract sense of edge is sharpness, acrimony; as, the edge of a satire.
4. Keenness of appetite or desire; as, to set the edge of appetite.
5. EDGE, v.t. To sharpen; to give a keen edge or point to.
corruption_summary: Hebrews 11 is read selectively, so that faith is expected always to escape the edge of the sword — and Jeremiah's abolished proverb returns as inherited guilt attached to a man by his ancestry.
corruption_paragraphs: Hebrews 11:34-37 is one paragraph, and preaching that stops at verse 35a produces a false doctrine. Faith stopped the mouths of lions and quenched the violence of fire; faith also was tortured, not accepting deliverance, was stoned, sawn asunder, slain with the sword, and wandered in sheepskins. The writer says these all obtained a good report through faith, and he means both lists. A gospel that promises the first outcome and hides the second sets its hearers up to conclude, at the first sword, that they had no faith. Jeremiah's proverb has also returned in modern dress. The claim that a man bears guilt for what his ancestors did — carried by lineage or by group rather than by his own act — is the sour-grape saying in a new accent. Ezekiel answers it in the same terms: the soul that sinneth, it shall die… the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father (Ezekiel 18:20).

The principle to recover is Ecclesiastes 10:10, which is the plainest verse in Scripture about working smarter. A blunt axe can be compensated for by strength, and men do it every day — more hours, more force, more strain — when the wise course is to stop and whet the edge. Solomon calls that wisdom, and the application reaches to prayer, study, and the ordering of a life. Much Christian exhaustion is a dull tool swung harder.
roots_summary: Hebrew peh is a mouth, and the sword's edge is its mouth; qatseh is an end or brink. Greek stoma likewise renders the edge of a sword in Hebrews 11:34.
roots_lines: Hebrew peh (H6310) — a mouth; idiomatically the edge of a sword, which devours.
Hebrew qatseh (H7097) — an end, extremity, brink; the edge of a border or territory.
Hebrew qahah (H6949) — to be blunt or set on edge; the teeth of Jeremiah 31:29.
Greek stoma (G4750) — a mouth; the edge of the sword in Hebrews 11:34, following the Hebrew idiom.
Greek distomos (G1366) — two-mouthed, two-edged; the sword of the word in Hebrews 4:12.
usage: Of battle won under intercession: discomfited Amalek and his people with the edge of the sword (Exodus 17:13).
Of faith that escapes it: escaped the edge of the sword, out of weakness were made strong (Hebrews 11:34).

pos: v. (to disperse, to drive apart; rendering Hebrew puts and zarah, Greek diaspeiro and skorpizo)
etymology: A variant of shatter, from Middle English. Hebrew zarah is properly to winnow — to throw grain into the wind so the chaff blows away — which gives the scattering of a people its agricultural and judicial overtone at once.
biblical_def: To scatter in Scripture is God's act before it is anyone else's, and it serves three purposes. It is judgment: at Babel “the LORD did there confound the language of all the earth: and from thence did the LORD scatter them abroad upon the face of all the earth” (Genesis 11:9) — a scattering that broke a united rebellion and, in breaking it, filled the earth as the original command had required. It is the mark of a people without a shepherd: Ezekiel indicts Israel's shepherds because the sheep “were scattered, because there is no shepherd: and they became meat to all the beasts of the field” (Ezekiel 34:5) — and that chapter ends with God promising to be the shepherd himself. It is prophesied of the disciples and fulfilled in a garden: “smite the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered: and I will turn mine hand upon the little ones” (Zechariah 13:7). Our Lord quotes it on the night he was betrayed, so that the scattering of his own men was foretold and did not surprise him. And it becomes the engine of the mission: after Stephen's death the church “were all scattered abroad throughout the regions of Judaea and Samaria” (Acts 8:1), and the next verses report that they went everywhere preaching the word. James writes to the result: “the twelve tribes which are scattered abroad” (James 1:1).
webster_summary: To disperse. God scatters at Babel in judgment, mourns a flock scattered for want of a shepherd, foretells his own disciples' scattering — and turns a persecution's scattering into the spread of the gospel.
webster_full: SCATTER, v.t. To disperse; to dissipate; to separate or remove things to a distance from each other.
2. To throw loosely about; to sprinkle; as, to scatter seed.
3. To spread or set thinly; as, to scatter trees over a field.
4. SCATTER, v.i. To be dispersed or dissipated.
5. In Scripture, to disperse a people; I will scatter them among the heathen, Lev. 26.
corruption_summary: Scattering is read only as loss, so that dispersion, exile, and the breaking up of what was gathered are treated as pure defeat — when Acts 8 shows God using a persecution's scattering to sow the word.
corruption_paragraphs: Every scattering in Scripture is painful and none is merely negative. Babel broke a project and thereby fulfilled the creation mandate to replenish the earth. The exile emptied a land and produced synagogues, a preserved text, and a people who never returned to idols. The persecution after Stephen emptied Jerusalem of its church and planted the gospel in Samaria and, before long, in Antioch, where disciples were first called Christians. Luke does not moralise about this; he simply reports that they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word (Acts 8:4). A congregation losing members to distance, or a work broken up, may be watching the same providence and should be slow to name it defeat.

The principle to recover is that the sheep scatter when the shepherd is struck, and that God says so beforehand. Zechariah 13:7 is a hard verse — the sword is summoned against the man that is God's fellow, which is a claim about the Messiah's deity — and Christ applies it to himself hours before it happened. The disciples' failure that night was foretold, atoned for, and repaired; he told them in the same breath that after he was risen he would go before them into Galilee. Ezekiel 34 gives the same comfort in the same order: the flock scattered for want of a shepherd, and then I will both search my sheep, and seek them out.
roots_summary: Hebrew puts is to scatter or dash in pieces; zarah is to winnow, to fan away. Greek diaspeiro gives diaspora; skorpizo is to disperse a flock.

Hebrew pazar (H6340) — to scatter abroad, to disperse; also to scatter gifts liberally.
Greek diaspeiro (G1289) — to sow throughout, to scatter; the root of diaspora, Acts 8:1.
Greek skorpizo (G4650) — to disperse; the wolf scattereth the sheep, John 10:12.
usage: Of judgment that fulfilled a mandate: did the LORD scatter them abroad upon the face of all the earth (Genesis 11:9).
Of a flock without a shepherd: they were scattered, because there is no shepherd (Ezekiel 34:5).
